passage: I'm Rashmi, and I live in the flat next door, so our balconies almost touch. Baljeet came into that house as a bride three weeks ago. I keep seeing the same picture: Baljeet washing steel glasses that are already clean, then asking the mother-in-law, “Is this how you like it?” The father-in-law reads his paper and says nothing. The mother-in-law answers, “Fine, fine,” without looking up, which leaves Baljeet asking again. Yesterday the husband, Sanjay, took the glasses gently. “I'll dry tonight, Ma,” he said, and stood beside Baljeet at the sink. I can't say what Baljeet feels. But the shoulders came down a little.

qa.q: What was Baljeet washing when Rashmi kept seeing the same picture?
qa.a: Baljeet was washing steel glasses that were already clean.

qa.q: What might Baljeet be feeling when asking, “Is this how you like it?” again and again?
qa.a: Baljeet seems anxious about being judged in the new house and is asking for approval, though Rashmi says the inner feeling can't be known for sure.

qa.q: What did Sanjay do that helped, and why might it matter?
qa.a: Sanjay took the glasses, offered to dry and stood beside Baljeet at the sink. A spouse who stands beside a newcomer shows the house that the two are together.

qa.q: How might the mother-in-law see Baljeet's repeated “Is this how you like it?”
qa.a: The mother-in-law may think the question needs no more than “Fine, fine,” and may not notice how unsure Baljeet feels, which is why the asking goes on.

grounding: An observer describes a newly married person joining a household with unspoken habits, feeling watched, and helped when the spouse stands beside them.

passage:
Day 2. In his wife's family home, Pranav was told which chair was his and that he must wait for the elders to eat first. He nodded and stayed silent. Her aunts asked about his salary, his mother's cooking and his plans for children. Pema kept passing him water.
Day 9. Her uncle corrected how he folded the newspaper. Pranav smiled tightly and refolded it. That evening Pema said to her father, “Papa, he's a guest and a family member both. Let him choose his chair.” Her father grunted, then laughed.
Day 30. Pranav's chair was the one by the window, and he had started asking the aunts for recipes.

qa.q: Which chair did Pranav's hosts tell him was his on Day 2?
qa.a: On Day 2 he was told which chair was his and that he must wait for the elders to eat first.

qa.q: Why did Pranav smile tightly and refold the newspaper on Day 9?
qa.a: Pranav seems to feel uncomfortable and judged in the new house, so he goes along quietly instead of objecting.

qa.q: What did Pema do that helped Pranav settle in?
qa.a: Pema kept passing him water, then spoke up to her father so that Pranav could choose his chair, standing beside him.

qa.q: How might Pema's father have seen the change by Day 30?
qa.a: Her father may have come to see Pranav as part of the family, since he laughed after the chair remark and by Day 30 Pranav sat by the window and asked the aunts for recipes.

grounding: A newly married man joins his wife's household, feels watched and evaluated on Days 2 and 9, and settles in by Day 30 with his wife beside him.

passage: Clara had been married to Anders for five weeks when they moved into the top floor of his parents' house outside Bergen while their own flat was being repaired. Nobody told her the rules, but there were rules. Coffee was at three, not ten past. Boots went on the left rack, never the right. When she loaded the dishwasher, her mother-in-law quietly reloaded it after she left the kitchen. Anders's sister watched Clara slice bread and said, 'Oh, you cut it thick.' Clara began to feel she was sitting an exam she hadn't studied for. One evening, after another reloaded dishwasher, Anders said at dinner, 'Mamma, Clara does it her way, and it works fine. Let's leave it.' His mother paused, then nodded. Clara's shoulders dropped for the first time that week.

qa.q: Where did Clara and Anders move while their flat was being repaired?
qa.a: Into the top floor of his parents' house outside Bergen.

qa.q: What was Clara feeling during her first weeks in the house?
qa.a: She felt self-conscious and uneasy, like sitting an exam she hadn't studied for, as her dishwasher loading and bread slicing were quietly corrected.

qa.q: What did Anders do that helped, and how could he keep helping?
qa.a: He calmly backed Clara's way at dinner; he could keep explaining the house habits to her and gently speak up when she is corrected.

qa.q: How might Anders's mother see the dishwasher business?
qa.a: She may see reloading it as simply keeping her kitchen right, not as a judgement, without realising how watched Clara feels.

grounding: A newly married woman joins a household full of unspoken rules, feels evaluated, and is helped when her husband stands beside her.

passage: Three months after the wedding, Hrithik started teaching physics at his in-laws' coaching institute in Indore. The staff room had rules nobody wrote down. Papaji, his father-in-law, always took the first cup of tea. Varun, his wife's elder brother, decided which batches got the air-conditioned rooms. On his first day, Hrithik sat in the chair by the window, and the room went silent. Varun said, 'That's Papaji's chair,' with a smile that wasn't really one. For weeks, Hrithik felt every lesson was being judged through the glass door. Then one evening his wife, Nidhi, came to the staff room and said to her brother, in front of everyone, 'Hrithik's batch scored best in the mock test. Give him a proper room.' Varun shrugged. The next Monday, Hrithik had the corner room.

qa.q: Which subject does Hrithik teach at the institute?
qa.a: Physics.

qa.q: How did Hrithik feel during his first weeks at the institute?
qa.a: He felt watched and judged, as if every lesson was assessed through the glass door, after the awkward moment with the chair.

qa.q: What could help Hrithik settle in faster?
qa.a: Asking Nidhi or a friendly colleague to explain the unwritten staff-room habits, and keeping up steady teaching while the family adjusts.

qa.q: How might Varun see Hrithik's arrival?
qa.a: Varun is used to deciding things there, so he may see Hrithik as a newcomer testing the family order, which is why he guards the chair and the rooms.

grounding: A new son-in-law working in his wife's family institute feels watched by settled habits until his wife stands up for him.

subtopic: Family systems (joint family, in-laws, favourite child, family roles and secrets)
passage:
Dear Seema,
Two months into married life in Nashik, and I'm still learning the house. Nobody said the lamp in the pooja room must be lit before tea, but Aai's face told me the first morning I got it wrong. My sister-in-law tastes the salt in whatever I cook, just a little, and says nothing. At the Sankranti gathering, three aunts watched me hand out til-gul as if they were marking a paper.
Some nights I cry quietly in the bathroom so nobody hears.
What keeps me going is Nikhil. Last Sunday, when his aunt asked why I still work, he said, 'Because she's good at it, and we decided together.' He also tells me the rules before I trip on them now.
Write soon. I miss our loud chai.
Irawati

qa.q: What must be lit before tea, according to the house's unspoken rule?
qa.a: The lamp in the pooja room.

qa.q: How does Irawati feel at the Sankranti gathering?
qa.a: She feels nervous and self-conscious, as if three aunts were marking a paper while she handed out til-gul.

qa.q: What is Nikhil doing that helps Irawati adjust?
qa.a: He stands up for her in front of the family and now tells her the house rules before she trips on them.

qa.q: What might the sister-in-law be thinking when she tastes the salt?
qa.a: She may be curious or protective of the family's way of cooking, testing the newcomer without realising how judged Irawati feels.

grounding: A new daughter-in-law describes feeling watched in a household of unspoken rules, and how her husband's support helps.

subtopic: Family systems (joint family, in-laws, favourite child, family roles and secrets)
passage: You asked how the first months went, Farah. Honestly? At the office I'm still Damini, but the day I married Chetan I became "bahu", and a bahu is watched. The first morning I made tea with ginger, the way my mother does. Chetan's mother took one sip, said nothing, and quietly made herself a fresh cup. His sister looked at me, then at the pot. His grandfather drank mine without a word, which I still don't know how to read. At dinner I started eating before Papa-ji picked up his roti. The whole table went still. My face was burning. Then Chetan tore his own roti and said, "We were both starving, Papa, blame me." Papa-ji laughed, and everyone breathed again. Nobody hands you the rules; you learn them from silences. It took most of a year. Last Sunday his mother asked me to make the tea for her sister's visit. Ginger and all.

qa.q: What did Damini put in the tea on her first morning?
qa.a: She made tea with ginger, the way her mother does.

qa.q: What was Damini feeling when the whole table went still at dinner?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and exposed; her face was burning because she had broken a rule nobody had told her about.

qa.q: Which choice of Chetan's helped, and why?
qa.a: Chetan took the blame with a light joke, so Damini was not left alone and his father could laugh instead of judging her.

qa.q: How might Chetan's mother have seen the ginger tea that first morning?
qa.a: It may have tasted like a stranger in her kitchen; making a fresh cup quietly let her keep her own way without a quarrel, and a year later she trusts Damini with the guests' tea.

grounding: Shows a new bahu feeling watched in her husband's household, learning its rules slowly, with Chetan standing beside her.
